title: Are they equal?
hookLine: are those who know and those who don't know equal (39:9)
carry: knowing isn't equal to not knowing

lines: IT STARTS IN THE MIDDLE OF THE NIGHT.
cards: Some questions don't need an answer. Is a full glass heavier than an empty one? Would you rather be warm or freezing?

A teacher asks one in class and nobody raises a hand, because the answer is sitting right there in the question. The Qur'an asks questions like this, and Surah Az-Zumar, the thirty-ninth, has one about knowing.
You might expect it to start in a classroom. It starts in the middle of the night.

teach.b: Verse nine opens with a picture. Someone is up in the hours of the night, prostrating and standing in prayer, wary of the hereafter, hoping for the mercy of their Lord. Is that person like the one who isn't?

teach.h: THOSE WHO KNOW, THOSE WHO DON'T.
teach.b: Pickthall: "Are those who know equal with those who know not? But only men of understanding will pay heed." The answer is built in: no. But look at what knowing means here.

It's not trivia. It sits right after the night prayer, the fear, the hope. Some commentators read the knowing in this verse as knowing your Lord and acting on it: the person who knows why they're awake in the night.
So the verse sets learning and devotion side by side, and the tradition took that seriously.

teach.h: A PATH TO KNOWLEDGE, A PATH TO PARADISE.
teach.b: A hadith in Sahih Muslim says that whoever walks a path seeking knowledge, Allah makes easy for them a path to paradise.
Another, in Ibn Majah, says seeking knowledge is an obligation on every Muslim, and scholars point out that this includes men and women alike.

Then the last phrase: only people of understanding, ulu'l-albab, will take it to heart. Albab is the plural of lubb, a kernel, the inner core of a nut. People of understanding get to the core of things.
Knowing and not knowing aren't the same, and the verse adds that it takes some knowing even to notice that.

how: Muslims treat seeking knowledge as a religious duty; many attend study circles (halaqas) at mosques, and 39:9 is quoted to encourage study.

o: a lamp lit for reading late at night
the heart's deep love for learning
a kernel, the inner core of a nut

games.q: the question in Az-Zumar — tap the pairs.
p: not equal to those who don't

s: the verse about knowing is set in a classroom
it comes right after someone praying in the night, wary and hopeful.
a hadith calls seeking knowledge an obligation on every Muslim
it's in Ibn Majah; scholars note every means men and women alike.
ulu'l-albab comes from a word for the kernel of a nut
lubb: the core. people of understanding get to the core.

games.q: the verse asks: are those who know equal with those who don't? what does it say right after?
o: yes, before God all are equal.
only people of understanding will take heed.
games.why: only ulu'l-albab, people of understanding, will take it to heart. it takes some knowing even to notice.

practice: If you have a book nearby, a Qur'an, a history, anything worth learning from, open it and read one page slowly, as if you'll be asked about it.
If not, think of one subject you've always meant to understand better, and the first thing you'd read about it. Then sit with what you read, or chose, and let it settle to its kernel.

wordCard.voice: Lubb, a kernel, the inner core of a nut, the root of ulu'l-albab, those who get to the core of things. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: are they equal? a question the Qur'an asks often, with the answer built in.

carryVoice: Your line: knowing isn't equal to not knowing. It starts with someone awake at night. Until tomorrow.
